subsection: 6. Case study: the secession of Katanga, 1960–1965

notes.h: Background: Katanga's mineral wealth and its politics before 1960
notes.b: Katanga was the richest province of the Belgian Congo, and its wealth was in the hands of a Belgian company. That wealth, and the ethnic politics that grew up around it, explain why the province tried to break away as soon as the Congo became independent.
points: Belgian rule had been paternalistic (the colonial power treated Africans like children to be guided): the Congo was Leopold II's Congo Free State and then the Belgian Congo from 1908. Few Congolese were educated, so there were almost no African officers or professionals at independence.

The Congo became independent on 30 June 1960 under President Kasa-Vubu and Prime Minister Lumumba, with its capital at Léopoldville. The army, the Force Publique, mutinied in early July and Belgian troops returned, so the new state was unstable from the start.

The crisis also unfolded during the Cold War, when the United States and the Soviet Union competed for influence in new states. The United Nations, led by its Secretary-General, tried to keep the Congo out of that rivalry.

Katanga, later called Shaba, was the copper-mining heart of the Congo and also produced cobalt and uranium. It was the richest province and supplied a very large share of the country's revenue, which gave its leaders a strong reason to want to keep that money.

The Union Minière du Haut-Katanga, a Belgian-controlled company, ran the mines. This is a transnational economy (companies and capital operating across borders): a foreign company shaped the province's economy, administration and politics.

Mining towns such as Élisabethville (now Lubumbashi), Kolwezi and Jadotville had a large European population, and Congolese workers lived in segregated housing. Belgian and settler interests backed Conakat because they wanted to keep Belgian influence.

Conakat (Confédération des associations tribales du Katanga) was formed in 1958 and came to be led by Moïse Tshombe, who was linked by marriage to the Lunda ruling family. It was strongest among the Lunda and campaigned for autonomy, even federalism, so that Katanga would keep its own revenue.

The rival Balubakat party, led by Jason Sendwe, drew support from the Baluba of northern Katanga and had links to Lumumba. Their rivalry is what the colonial and later term tribalism (ethnic loyalty) describes, though historians stress that politics and economics mattered as well as ethnicity.
notes.tip: For the 30 and 40-mark answers, name the Union Minière, Tshombe and Conakat. Do not give a percentage for Katanga's share of revenue: say copper, cobalt, uranium and a very large share.

notes.h: The secession and Belgian backing, July 1960
notes.b: Only eleven days after independence, Katanga declared itself a separate state. A secession is the breaking away of part of a state, and this one was backed by Belgium, so it became an international problem at once.
points: Tshombe proclaimed Katanga independent on 11 July 1960, eleven days after the Congo's independence. This is separate from the South Kasai secession of August 1960 and from the army mutiny.

In the May 1960 provincial elections Conakat formed the provincial government with Tshombe as president of the province, while in the national results Lumumba's allies were strong. Katanga's leaders therefore feared being ruled by Lumumba's government in Léopoldville.

Tshombe's reasons were to keep Katanga's revenue in the province, because it was so large, and to avoid a centralising government in Léopoldville which he called Communist and controlled by outsiders.

Belgian troops intervened from 10 July 1960, the day before the proclamation, and Belgium gave Katanga military and technical help. Belgian officers and advisers and paid foreign mercenaries trained and led the Katanga Gendarmerie (Katanga's army and police).
No state recognised Katanga, so its claim to be independent was weak, and Lumumba's government saw the secession as a threat to the unity of the Congo.
Lumumba appealed to the United Nations to help restore the Congo's territory. The Security Council set up ONUC, the UN force in the Congo, in July 1960 (resolution of 14 July).

On 9 August 1960 the Security Council called on Belgium to withdraw from Katanga, and UN troops entered the province on 12 August. Belgian troops withdrew after the UN arrived, but Belgian officers and advisers stayed on in the Katangan forces.
notes.tip: Short questions ask which province seceded, what Belgium sent and why the UN came. Give the date 11 July 1960 and say Belgium sent troops to protect its interests.

notes.b: The Katanga crisis destroyed Lumumba. When the UN would not defeat the secession, he looked to the Soviet Union, which alarmed the West and led to his removal and death in Katanga itself.
points: Lumumba was angry that ONUC would not use force against Tshombe. In August 1960 he accepted Soviet transport aircraft and trucks, which were used in an offensive in South Kasai, and this raised Western alarm about Cold War involvement in the Congo.
President Kasa-Vubu dismissed Lumumba on 5 September 1960. Lumumba declared Kasa-Vubu deposed, and on 14 September Colonel Mobutu's coup 'neutralised' both men, meaning it put both out of action.
Lumumba was confined to his residence under UN guard, left UN protection in late November 1960 and was arrested by Mobutu's troops in early December.
On 17 January 1961 he was flown to Katanga and killed, with Belgian officers present and Katangan leaders taking part. His death was announced on 13 February 1961.
The murder provoked Soviet and African protests and riots in several capitals. It also led to Security Council Resolution 161 of February 1961, which authorised the use of force as a last resort.
Lumumba became a martyr of African nationalism, which means he was honoured as a hero who died for African independence.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the men: Kasa-Vubu was president, Lumumba prime minister, Tshombe Katanga's leader and Mobutu the army chief. Learn the dates 5 and 14 September 1960 and 17 January 1961.

notes.h: The UN operation and the Irish troops, 1960–1961
notes.b: ONUC was meant to restore order, not to take sides. Its rule of staying out of internal disputes left it unable to end the secession, until events in 1961 pushed it into force and put Irish soldiers in the front line.
points: ONUC was the UN force sent to the Congo under Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld. It lasted 1960–64, and the UN declared it would not intervene in internal disputes except to prevent civil war, which is why Lumumba was angry that it would not use force against Katanga.
On 8 November 1960 an Irish patrol was ambushed at Niemba by Baluba tribesmen, and nine Irish soldiers were killed. Niemba was an ambush in 1960, whereas Jadotville was a siege in 1961.

Security Council Resolution 161 of 21 February 1961 authorised force as a last resort to prevent civil war, and called for foreign military personnel and mercenaries to leave. Resolution 169 of 24 November 1961 explicitly authorised action against the secession and the mercenaries.

Conor Cruise O'Brien, an Irish diplomat and the UN representative in Katanga in 1961, pushed for a firmer policy. Operation Rumpunch on 28 August 1961 was followed by Operation Morthor, launched on 13 September 1961 to arrest the foreign officers and take control of Élisabethville. Morthor failed.

At Jadotville, 155 men of A Company, 35th Battalion, under Commandant Pat Quinlan, were besieged from 13 September 1961 by Katangan gendarmes with foreign mercenaries. With no relief, little water and low ammunition they surrendered on 17 September.
No Irish soldier was killed at Jadotville, and the men were held prisoner for about a month.
O'Brien later wrote of his Katanga experience in To Katanga and Back (1962). The UN's Congo operation cost about 250 lives, among them about 26 Irish soldiers.
notes.tip: Know the difference between Rumpunch (August 1961), Morthor (13 September 1961) and Grand Slam (December 1962), and between Resolutions 161 and 169. Morthor was launched on 13 September, not 24 September.

notes.h: The death of Hammarskjöld and the end of secession, 1961–1963
notes.b: After Morthor failed, the UN lost its Secretary-General in a plane crash and then, under his successor, finally defeated Katanga's forces. The Cold War also hung over this period.
points: At the UN General Assembly in autumn 1960 Nikita Khrushchev attacked Hammarskjöld's handling of the Congo and proposed replacing the Secretary-General with a three-man body (a troika). This was a sign of Soviet hostility to the UN's role.

Hammarskjöld's plane crashed near Ndola in Northern Rhodesia in the night of 17–18 September 1961, while he was travelling to meet Tshombe. The cause remains disputed, so do not state that it was sabotage.

Fighting between UN and Katangan forces in Élisabethville in December 1961 ended with the Kitona Declaration of 21 December 1961. Tshombe seemed to accept Katanga's place in the Congo, but he later repudiated it (rejected it).
U Thant succeeded Hammarskjöld as Secretary-General and continued the operation. Operation Grand Slam against the Katangan forces began on 28 December 1962.
Tshombe announced the end of the secession at Kolwezi on 14 January 1963, and UN troops entered Kolwezi a week later. He announced this after Operation Grand Slam, not as a negotiated settlement.
Tshombe then left for exile. The secession had lasted about two and a half years, and its end removed the largest threat to the central government's authority.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Hammarskjöld (died September 1961) with U Thant, his successor. Say the cause of the crash is disputed, and that the secession ended in January 1963.

notes.h: Tshombe, Mobutu and the Congo's new order, 1963–1965
notes.b: Defeating the secession did not bring stability. Tshombe returned as national prime minister, the east rose in rebellion and the army, under Mobutu, took over.
points: Tshombe was recalled as prime minister of the Congo in July 1964 and held the post until Kasa-Vubu dismissed him in October 1965. The UN force left in 1964, leaving the army more important.

The Simba rebellion of 1964, by supporters of Lumumba, spread through the east. Stanleyville fell in August 1964, and in November 1964 Belgian paratroopers, carried by American aircraft, rescued hostages there. The rebellion was crushed in 1964-65 with the help of mercenaries.
Mobutu seized power on 24 November 1965, so this was his second coup, after that of 14 September 1960 which handed power back to Kasa-Vubu in 1961.
Tshombe went into exile in Spain. His plane was hijacked to Algeria in 1967 and he died in custody there in 1969.
The secession had shown the importance of the army and of foreign support, and Mobutu's coup used the army to end the factional fighting of the 1960s, which is why army rule followed.

In 1977 and 1978 former Katangan gendarmes based in Angola invaded Shaba province. The 1977 invasion was repelled with Moroccan troops and a French airlift, and in 1978 French and Belgian paratroops retook Kolwezi.
The United States supported Mobutu's regime with military aid after 1965, which made the army a key instrument of Cold War policy in central Africa.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Tshombe as Katanga's leader (1960-63) with Tshombe as prime minister of the whole Congo (1964-65).

notes.b: Born Joseph-Désiré Mobutu on 14 October 1930 at Lisala, he served in the Force Publique (the colonial army) and worked as a journalist before independence. He rose to become dictator of the Congo, which he renamed Zaire, and ruled until 1997. Within this topic, his importance is that the crisis of 1960-65 gave him the army, Western backing and the means to take power.
points: He was chief of staff of the Congolese army from July 1960 and led the coup of 14 September 1960 that 'neutralised' Lumumba and Kasa-Vubu. His troops arrested Lumumba in December 1960, and he handed power back to Kasa-Vubu in February 1961.

As a direct participant he worked with the CIA station chief Larry Devlin in 1960, and the United States saw him as the best anti-communist leader. The Church Committee of the US Senate in 1975 later revealed CIA plans against Lumumba.

He was shaped by events: the crisis gave him control of the army and Western backing, and it taught him the dangers of fragmentation. He seized power again on 24 November 1965, and foreign support helped keep him in power.
He had four politicians hanged in public in June 1966, founded his Popular Movement of the Revolution (MPR) in 1967 and ruled as president under a one-party system.

He nationalised the Union Minière's Katanga assets in 1966-67, creating Gécamines. He launched the policy of authenticité (a return to African authenticity) in 1971, renamed the Congo Zaire in 1971 and took the name Mobutu Sese Seko in 1972.
Contemporaries in the West, including the United States and Belgium, regarded him as a bulwark against communism in central Africa, whereas many Congolese saw a corrupt ruler who enriched his circle.
Historians describe personal dictatorship and kleptocracy (rule by theft): he drew on mineral revenues and Western aid, rewarded loyalists and kept the state weak.

Only the period to 1990 belongs to this topic: in April 1990 he announced the end of the one-party state, and his Western support weakened with the end of the Cold War. He was overthrown in May 1997 by Laurent-Désiré Kabila and died in exile in Morocco in September 1997.
notes.tip: For a question on Mobutu, give his career (army chief, two coups, the one-party state, Zaire, corruption, Western support) with dates, and say what an opponent and a supporter would say.

notes.b: The secession mattered inside the Congo, where it tested whether the state could survive, and far beyond it, where it involved the UN, the superpowers and the African states.
points: Nationally, the secession tested whether the Congo could survive as one state, and the central government's victory preserved its territory. However, the state stayed weak and dominated by the army.
Internationally, the crisis was a Cold War contest in which the United States and the Soviet Union, and the former colonial power Belgium, supported different sides.
The Katanga case set a precedent for the UN's involvement in internal conflicts and for its peacekeeping role (using troops to keep order between rival forces).
This differs from Suez, where a UN force separated combatants, because in the Congo the UN used force on a member state's territory.
Mobutu nationalised the Union Minière's Katangan assets in 1966-67 and set up the state company Gécamines, so the province's mineral wealth became the central state's main source of revenue.

African states divided: the Casablanca group, including Ghana, Guinea and Egypt, backed Lumumba and the central government. The crisis was one of the first tests of African unity before the Organisation of African Unity was founded in 1963.
The cost of the operation caused a UN financial crisis because the Soviet Union and France refused to pay towards it, and the death of Hammarskjöld showed the risks to the UN itself.
notes.tip: For national versus international significance, say nationally the Congo kept its territory but stayed weak and army-dominated, and internationally there was a UN precedent, a financial crisis and the death of a Secretary-General.

notes.h: Assessment: why Katanga seceded and why it drew international involvement
notes.b: Examiners reward an argument that ranks the causes and weighs success against limits, and contemporary views against later ones. These paired points give you that material.
points: Cause: Katanga's mineral revenues, held by the Belgian-controlled Union Minière, gave its leaders a strong economic reason to keep control of their wealth, and Belgian companies and officials supported that aim.

Cause: Conakat claimed that Katanga's peoples had a separate regional identity, and fear of Lumumba's centralising government strengthened regional loyalties. This is why Belgian backing mattered so much to the outcome.

International involvement came from Belgian self-interest in protecting its investments, Cold War rivalry (the Soviet aid to Lumumba and the CIA role) and the UN's duty to protect a member state's territory.
Achievement: the central government's victory kept the Congo's borders as drawn at independence, in line with the African principle of accepting colonial frontiers.
Limit: the Congo became dependent on foreign military support, and the Simba rebellion of 1964 and then army rule showed how much remained unstable.

Contemporary view: the central government, much of Africa and the Soviet bloc saw the secession as a neo-colonial plot, while Tshombe and his supporters saw it as self-determination against centralised rule.
Contemporary view of the UN: the Soviet bloc and some African states accused it of failing to protect Lumumba and the central government.

Later view: Ludo De Witte's book on Lumumba's murder prompted a Belgian parliamentary inquiry, which reported in 2001 that Belgian ministers and officials bore moral responsibility. Historians stress the roles of Belgium and the Union Minière in sustaining Katanga.
notes.tip: The 100-mark essay asks why Katanga seceded, why it drew in outsiders and what the results were. State a thesis ranking causes (wealth and the Union Minière, Conakat, Belgian backing, fear of Lumumba), then develop each. A narrative of UN operations without analysis scores poorly.

An economy in which companies and capital operate across national borders, as with the Union Minière's control of Katangan mining.
The withdrawal of a region from a state to form a separate state, as Katanga did from July 1960 to January 1963.
The Belgian-controlled mining company that ran Katanga's copper, cobalt and uranium industries.
A foreign soldier paid to fight for a state or faction, who served in the Katanga Gendarmerie and against the UN forces.
The rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union from 1945 to 1991, which shaped the Katanga crisis and the Congo's politics.
Mobutu's policy from 1971 to promote African culture and names, and to reject European influence.
The deployment of UN forces to keep order and separate combatants, as in ONUC in the Congo from 1960.
The state mining company created in 1967 out of the Union Minière's Katanga assets after Mobutu nationalised them.
The mining town in Katanga where Tshombe announced the end of the secession in January 1963, and which French and Belgian paratroops recaptured in 1978.
The name Mobutu gave the Congo in 1971, used until his overthrow in 1997.
